title: Raise the price 10%: more money or less?
hook: Two sellers raise prices by the same 10%. Do they both take in more?

knows: that buyers buy less when the price rises
that revenue is price times the amount sold
doesNotKnow: that whether a price rise adds revenue depends on how much buyers cut back

misconception: A price rise always cuts sales enough to hurt, or never does.
objective: The learner can explain that revenue is price times sales, so a price rise adds revenue when buyers barely cut back (salt: +8.9%) and loses it when they cut back a lot (tickets: −12%).

claims.text: A 10% price rise with a 1% cut in purchases (salt) leaves revenue at 1.1 × 0.99 = 1.089 of before: +8.9%.
A 10% price rise with a 20% cut (concert tickets) leaves revenue at 1.1 × 0.8 = 0.88 of before: −12%.
The buyers' reactions are invented example sensitivities (salt buyers cut 0.1% and ticket buyers 2% per 1% price rise, in a straight line), not measured data.
claims.source: Demo.tsx GOODS. At the slider's other settings: salt +30% → revenue 1.3 × 0.97 = 1.261; tickets +30% → 1.3 × 0.4 = 0.52.

claims.text: How strongly buyers' purchases react to a price change is called the price elasticity of demand.
claims.source: Standard definition, e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 5 (elasticity and its application).

claims.text: The lesson is a model: invented reactions, one price step, revenue (money taken in), not profit.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: invented buyers, revenue not profit'.

recall.question: A seller raises its price 20% and sales fall 5%. What happens to revenue?
recall.why: Revenue is price × sales: 1.2 × 0.95 = 1.14. Buyers barely reacted, so the higher price wins.
